true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently replaces the max_width/max_height variant

The PR adds a 4-argument `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` while the existing `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 is still present. In Ruby the later definition wins, so the 5-argument form is gone. Any caller still using `downsize(from, to, w, h, opts)` now raises ArgumentError or passes the wrong arguments. true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

This applies to attachments too, so the `max_attachment_size_kb` setting no longer has any effect on the client. Admins who lowered the limit will see files accepted client-side and rejected only later by the server, and admins who raised it will be blocked at 10MB. false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsizing applies to every image type and never checks the result against the limit

The loop only tries 5 passes, and after the loop the size is not rechecked. If the image is still over `max_image_size_kb`, the code continues to `Upload.create_for` with no explicit error, so the failure reason is unclear to the user. Also, the 80% scale is applied to non-animated formats such as SVG, where it may do nothing or produce unexpected output.

Downsizing writes the output over its own input file and ignores failures

`OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, ...)` uses the same path as source and destination. ImageMagick reads and writes the same file, which is fragile and can corrupt the upload. `convert_with` returns false on failure, but the return value is ignored, so the loop just retries up to 5 times on an unchanged file. A failed conversion should stop the loop and fall through to a clear error. Writing to a separate temp file and swapping on success would be safer.

The diff does not show such a search.

Bullet margin-top rule removed from extra-info badges with no replacement

Nothing in the PR confirms that the names are unique or that the output of existing callers is unchanged.

The description says only 'Test 5', and the title says the change optimizes header layout performance. Panel float removed and replaced with flex ordering that is not verified

`.panel` drops `float: right` and gains `margin-left: auto` plus `order(3)`. This only works if every sibling in `.contents` is a flex item with orders 1 and 2 set correctly. Siblings like `#site-logo` and `.icons` are not given any order, so the final arrangement depends on DOM order and browser support for the old `-webkit-box-ordinal-group` fallback. Removing the .title float rule changes header layout without replacement

The diff deletes the `.title { float: left; }` rule from `.d-header .contents` and switches `.contents` to a flex container. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

Each of these exercises a distinct branch of `website_name`, and the trailing-slash case currently produces an incorrect result.

For a website such as `http://example.com/`, `URI(...).path` is `/`, so `website_name` becomes `example.com/` when the discourse host matches. The path logic is also repeated in three branches, so this edge case is duplicated and easy to miss. Normalize the path (e.g. treat `/` as empty) before concatenating.

`website` is listed in `untrusted_attributes`, so for a TL0 user viewed by an anonymous guardian, `include_website?` returns false and the website is hidden. The new `website_name` attribute is not covered: `include_website_name` only checks `website.present?` and never calls `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`. As a result the website host, and now the full path, is still serialized for those users, bypassing the trust-level restriction. Default autofix tuning changed from 'low' to 'off' globally

DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT and the project option default both change from 'low' to 'off', silently disabling autofix automation for all existing projects that rely on the default, with no migration or changelog and no clear product reason in the PR description.

Error IDs from the replay query are used without checking response shape; project_id unrelated

`response[0].get("error_ids", [])` assumes process_raw_response returns a list of dicts for the replay; if the query returns no rows or error_ids is None, `error_ids` becomes None and is passed to fetch_error_details which iterates it, raising TypeError. The endpoint then 500s instead of degrading to no error context.

Error events fetched with default placeholders when data missing

`data.get("timestamp", 0.0)` defaults missing timestamps to 0, so error events with no timestamp are placed at the start of the timeline by gen_request_data rather than being skipped or handled explicitly.

Gradient change alters appearance of right mask

The transparent right-mask gradient changes from a white rgba pair to theme background, altering visuals in dark themes without a corresponding design justification.

Logging event_data uses the workflow-specific event data variable

The extra field renamed from event_data to workflow_event_data changes the logged payload; this is a behavior change in logs but the diff does not explain it and the earlier group-level event_data reference is lost for debugging.

Migration body replaced with no-op for an already-applied/parallel migration

The data migration 0917 is rewritten to `return` immediately, and 0920 is likewise gutted. If any environment already ran the original 0917 or 0920, their data conversion is silently skipped on future runs; and the comment references 0921_convert_org_saved_searches_to_views_rerevised, which is not part of this PR. Removing the real conversion without adding the referenced migration means org saved searches are never converted.

Owner handling in update() uses validated_data.get('owner') but create() does not validate owner belongs to org

The owner field is accepted from user input and written directly to owner_user_id/owner_team_id without verifying the user or team belongs to the detector's organization or project. A caller could assign an owner outside the organization (the test test_owner_not_in_organization asserts rejection, but the validator adds no such check).

Prompt tells LLM the output limit but is not enforced; 'AT MOST 55 words' conflicts with max_output_tokens=150

The prompt text was rewritten with contradictory guidance (for example 'Don't make overly generic statements' combined with the instruction to base summaries on 'proportional' themes), and the hard 55-word limit is only stated in the prompt, not enforced by parse_response. Output length is unchecked.

Query key omits environment and type dependency inconsistencies; attributes can be stale

The useQuery queryKey is derived from makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions which excludes environment, while the queryFn uses a separately-computed projectIds; changing projects through `projects` prop vs selection can cause cached results to be returned for the wrong project set.

Regex experiments removed but parameterization of ParameterizationRegex still referenced

The ParameterizationRegexExperiment class and its branch in parametrize_w_experiments are removed, yet the `ParameterizationExperiment` type alias now only covers callable experiments. Any configured regex experiment (or the traceparent experiment option removed from options/defaults.py) would now fail at runtime with an AttributeError on `.run` taking a callback of the wrong type, and the removed option could still be referenced in code paths reading it.

Removed Type rows from grouping variant display

The 'Type' row with explanatory tooltips is removed from every variant type, losing information (variant type and explanation) that users used to see in the grouping info panel.

Strict validation now rejects reports that were previously accepted

The endpoint used to accept any report dict and only record metrics. It now returns 422 for the whole batch if any single report fails validation (e.g., both timestamp and age present, unknown type, invalid URL). Browsers sending a batch will lose all metrics for a single malformed report, and the stricter `url`/`user_agent` requirements may reject real-world reports.

Writable aggregate fields filtered with isBaseVisualize but read via yAxes

The writable branch now filters by isBaseVisualize and flatMaps `visualize.yAxes`, while the readable branch uses `yAxis`; the mixing of Visualize (single yAxis) and BaseVisualize (yAxes) shapes means writable aggregate fields containing Visualize instances (which have yAxis, not yAxes) will be dropped from field refs.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is not atomic, allowing replay

The code checks the backup code index, then later writes back the re-encrypted array with the used code nulled, in a separate non-transactional update. Two concurrent login requests with the same valid backup code can both pass the indexOf check before either write lands, so one backup code can be used twice. The code is single-use by design, so this breaks the security guarantee.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup code errors are shown via next-auth result but the error message path for SecondFactorRequired still relies on ErrorCode mapping that drops IncorrectBackupCode in errorMessages

The new branches set error text directly, but the Lost access flow never resets twoFactorRequired on credential errors, and when a backup code is wrong the TwoFactor totp input is not shown, so the user cannot see the field they must fix. The error message localization keys are also added only to en/common.json, so other locales fall back to raw keys.

Backup code verification is not consumed and the disable path accepts an unvalidated body value

req.body.backupCode.replaceAll is called on a value that may not be a string (JSON body can send a number or object), which throws a 500 instead of a clean error. Also the used backup code is never consumed here, but the subsequent update wipes all backup codes anyway, so this is acceptable only if disabling is the sole consumer; the reliance on the later update is implicit and fragile.

Backup codes stored as encrypted blob in plain TEXT column without versioning

The codes are JSON encrypted with the global CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY. Rotating the key makes all stored backup codes unreadable, and the authorize and disable paths throw an internal error rather than prompting regeneration. No migration path or key rotation handling is provided.

Blob URL created on every setup call but revoked only against stale state

backupCodesUrl is read from closure state inside handleSetup, so if the user retries setup in the same render cycle the revoke may target a stale URL and leak or revoke the wrong object URL. The download link may then point to a revoked URL.

JSON.parse of decrypted backup codes can throw unhandled

If the stored backupCodes is corrupted or the decryption key changed, symmetricDecrypt or JSON.parse throws, producing an unhandled exception and a 500 with no ErrorCode. The same unguarded parse exists in next-auth-options.ts authorize, where it aborts login with an unmapped error.

No test covers backup code login, the core feature of this PR

The only tests exercise TOTP enable and disable plus backup download UI. Nothing verifies that a backup code logs in, that a used code is rejected on reuse, or that a wrong code shows the new error. The TODO acknowledges this, yet the PR checklist claims no tests were added.

Setup overwrites existing backup codes before enable, invalidating the previous set on abandoned setup

Backup codes are written to the DB at setup time while twoFactorEnabled is still false. If the user abandons enrollment, the previously stored codes are replaced anyway, and the codes shown to the user are only persisted, not confirmed. Also, codes are generated even if the user never completes the TOTP step, so the displayed codes can be out of sync with what is stored if setup is called twice (the second call overwrites the first set the user may have already saved).

Unrelated tabIndex change on password visibility toggle

Adding tabIndex={-1} to the show/hide password button in the shared PasswordField removes it from keyboard tab order across the whole app, an accessibility regression unrelated to backup codes and not described in the PR.

Used backup code is set to null, but indexOf of a null entry and remaining codes are not validated

Setting backupCodes[index] = null keeps the array length, and the stored JSON contains nulls. Submitting an empty or whitespace string after replaceAll can match a null entry only if the input is null, which is not possible from a string, so this is mostly safe, but a user submitting an input that is the empty string bypasses the check because credentials.backupCode is falsy and falls back to TOTP. More concretely, the truthiness check on backupCode means an attacker-supplied backupCode of an empty string skips backup verification entirely; the backup-code path is only reached when the field is non-empty.

backupCodes state typed as untyped empty array

useState([]) infers never[] under strict typing and the later assignment from body.backupCodes is untyped (any), weakening type safety for the displayed and downloaded codes.

Booking destinationCalendar connects only the first entry

Patch call uses selectedCalendar which may be undefined

Primary flag computed from the first destination only

Recurring cancel path reuses outer calendar and ignores per-reference credential

Inside the recurring branch the inner `calendar` variable shadows the outer one, and the deletion loop for every credential uses `updBooking.references` without matching credentialId. Deletions may target the wrong calendar account for collective bookings.

Team destination calendars pushed into evt.destinationCalendar for collective events without dedupe

`teamDestinationCalendars` is filled from `users.slice(1)` and then appended to `evt.destinationCalendar`. Team member objects gain firstName/lastName and lose nothing, but email fallback changed

The teamMemberPromises mapping adds empty firstName/lastName fields and changes `user.email || ""` to `?? ""`, and the comment now says the organizer is not a team member even for non-team events where users.slice(1) may be used. loadUsers swallows and remaps errors, and changes the hosts-empty fallback

The rewritten loadUsers throws a generic HttpError 500 for any unexpected error, hiding the real cause. The dynamic-user branch now throws if the list is empty, where it previously returned an empty list. The hosts branch returns `users.length ? users : eventType.users`, which changes which users are loaded when hosts exist but are empty. true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricated refresh_token placeholder is persisted

When refresh_token is missing, the function writes the literal string "refresh_token" into the returned data. Callers then store this in the credential key, replacing a real refresh token with a bogus value so future refreshes fail with an opaque error rather than a clear one.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Computed zod keys make the minimum schema match nothing useful

The keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` are not valid zod key definitions; `z.string().toString()` evaluates to the string "ZodString" (or similar), so the object shape validates a literal property named like that rather than an expiry number or arbitrary extra fields. The intended 'any property with a number is the expiry' check does not exist, so the minimal sync path does not validate expiry_date and may silently accept or reject token responses incorrectly.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sync path returns raw fetch Response and skips the token refresh entirely

When sync is enabled, the function fetches the endpoint and returns the Response, but callers such as google, hubspot, zoho and zohocrm then read `.data` (axios shape) or call the refresh function's result shape. A fetch Response has no `.data`, so token fields are undefined and the stored credential is corrupted. Also the response is not checked for `ok` status.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Refresh failure checks statusText instead of response.ok

The check `response.statusText !== "OK"` is fragile (HTTP/2 responses have empty statusText) and wrongly treats failures as errors or successes. Use response.ok and surface the error body.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Schema parse throws instead of returning 400

appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse throws a ZodError on invalid bodies, which Next.js reports as a 500 rather than a client error. safeParse with a 400 response is expected here.

false_negatives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

false_positives.candidate:
APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean

The expression `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` evaluates to a string or undefined. Its use in conditionals works, but the exported type is wrong and the flag is truthy for any non-empty value, so the .env.example placeholder `""` values are strings that are truthy only when both are non-empty; the type should be coerced to boolean.

Credential lookup by appId uses wrong identifier, risking duplicate credentials

The lookup and create use appMetadata.slug, but the create sets type: appMetadata.type. Existing credentials created by OAuth callbacks use differing type values (e.g. google_calendar vs app slug), so findFirst may miss the existing record and create duplicates, and the findFirst is not scoped by type.

Decryption failure and bad JSON cause unhandled 500s and no validation of key shape

symmetricDecrypt and JSON.parse run outside any try/catch; a wrong encryption key or malformed payload throws and returns a 500 with a stack trace. The decrypted object is also written to the DB without any schema validation for the target app.

Duplicate and unordered env entries

INTERCOM_SECRET is already listed twice in globalEnv, and the new entries are inserted out of alphabetical order (CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET after CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY), which will be flagged by the sorted-list check and makes the duplicate harder to spot.

Empty doc comment and misnamed handler docs

The `/** */` above the handler is empty, providing no documentation for a new public webhook endpoint that changes credential data.

Expiry computed from expires_in which may be missing on sync responses

key.expiry_date is computed as Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000 but the sync path's minimal schema does not require expires_in, so the result can be NaN, which then makes isTokenValid always false and refresh loops.

Google refresh reads token fields from a value that may be a Response

res?.data is read from refreshOAuthTokens' return, which in sync mode is a fetch Response with no .data, so token.access_token and token.expiry_date become undefined and the credential is overwritten with undefined token fields.

Hardcoded redirect URI breaks the slug-based pattern and the appConfig reference

The redirect URI was changed from `${appConfig.slug}` to a literal 'zoho-bigin'. This is equivalent today but diverges from the callback which still uses appConfig.slug, and it is an unrelated behavioral edit inside a refactor PR.

Header name comment and placeholder values are misleading

CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME says it should be lowercase, but the handler reads req.headers with a lookup key, which is case-sensitive only in the sense Node lowercases headers; the comment should state this. CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is also not documented to say it receives unauthenticated user tokens.

Lark sync path response is passed to handleLarkError but the sync endpoint returns form-encoded params

The sync request sends URLSearchParams with calcomUserId and appSlug, while the Lark handler expects a Lark-shaped JSON response (code, data.access_token). The sync endpoint contract is not reflected in the code, so handleLarkError will fail on any sync response that lacks a Lark envelope.

No tests added for new webhook, sync, or refresh behavior

The PR adds a credential-writing webhook, a new encryption path, and changes to every OAuth refresh path, yet no tests were added; the checklist itself states none were written. The refresh-path changes in particular touch many providers and need coverage.

Removed error logging for invalid refresh responses

The diff deletes the console.error for a failed zod parse of the refresh response, so Microsoft error responses are now silently swallowed and the credential keeps stale tokens with no diagnostic.

Salesforce refresh always happens and prisma is not imported

getClient now performs a token refresh on every construction, even when the access token is still valid, adding a network call per service instance. Also `prisma` is used at line 96 but is not imported in this file, so it will fail to compile/run.

Sync endpoint is called without authentication

The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only userId and appSlug with no secret or auth header, so anyone who can reach the endpoint configuration path can request tokens for any user id; the shared secret used by the inbound webhook is not reused here.

Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time equality

The header value is compared with !== against CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET. If the env var is unset and the header is also missing, undefined === undefined passes the check, allowing unauthenticated credential writes. The comparison should also be timing-safe and reject when the secret is empty.

Zoom refresh now accepts unvalidated responses in sync mode

parseRefreshTokenResponse uses the minimal schema when sync is enabled, so the zoom path no longer enforces scope and token_type, and key.expiry_date is later set from expires_in which may be undefined in the sync path, producing NaN expiry.

isTokenValid logic is inverted in existing code and now feeds the refresh path unchanged

isTokenValid returns true when expiresIn-or-expiryDate is less than now, i.e. when the token is expired, yet getToken calls refresh only when !isTokenValid. The refresh call is also wrapped in a function that swallows errors, so failures leave a stale token with no signal to callers.

refreshOAuthTokens receives credential.userId but credential is not in scope

Inside zohoCrmAuth the argument `credential.userId` refers to the outer parameter, which is fine, but the refreshed token expiry is set to Date.now()+60*60 without using expires_in, so tokens are marked valid for a fixed hour regardless of the real lifetime, and the sync path's Response object has no .data so zohoCrmTokenInfo.data is undefined.

Edited-step reminders deleted with forEach(async ...) and not awaited; scheduled rows still reference deleted data

The PR changes cancellation semantics across booking cancel, reschedule, workflow edit, and cron, yet adds no tests covering the cancelled flag, the 100-pending-cancellation failure mode, or the 1-hour cron window.

The loop calls client.request for each reminder inside a single try. Rescheduled booking's reminders are cancelled with immediateDelete=true for email but not awaited

await used inside a non-async callback context

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check rejects any slot that falls outside any single working-hours range

The working-hours guard uses `workingHours.find(...)` and returns false if the callback is truthy. The callback is truthy whenever one particular range does not contain the slot. So for a day with several ranges (for example 9-12 and 14-18, or aggregated hours from multiple hosts), a slot inside one range is rejected because it is outside another. The intended semantics is 'outside all ranges', which needs `every`/`some` logic. Also `end` is computed from `slotStartTime` instead of the slot end, so `end > workingHour.endTime` checks the start, not the end. Finally, the comparison uses UTC day and hour while `WorkingHours` values are minutes in the organizer timezone (per the type doc), so the check is evaluated in the wrong timezone. This is a regression that can remove valid slots for any multi-range or cross-timezone schedule.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Comparing dayjs objects with === is always false

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares object identity, not time. The branch that treats a zero-length override as a special case never runs. Use `.isSame(...)` or compare `valueOf()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Date override logic accepts partially overlapping slots and rejects slots when several overrides share a day

`dateOverrideExist` is set true for any override on the same day, and `find` returns true (meaning 'reject') as soon as any override on that day does not contain the slot. Consequences: (1) with two overrides on the same day, a slot inside override A is rejected because it is outside override B. (2) A slot that starts before an override's start and ends after it (partial overlap) matches none of the rejection conditions. It falls through to `return true` and is accepted even though it is not fully inside the override. The containment test must be: slot start >= override start and slot end <= override end, evaluated across all overrides for the day, with a clear rule for when no override covers the slot.

New timezone test does not exercise the bug it claims to cover

The added test asserts that the same UTC slots are returned for the attendee timezone +6:00 as for +5:30. It reuses the existing expectation, so it passes whether or not overrides are adjusted correctly. It does not cover the reported case: an organizer override whose organizer timezone differs from the schedule timezone, where the attendee's timezone should change which slots appear. No test covers the round-robin fixed-host override fix either, which is the primary change in the description.

Organizer timezone offset sign looks inverted for override conversion

`utcOffset = dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1` negates the organizer's offset. For Asia/Kolkata (+330) this shifts the override by -330 minutes, so the local day of the override is computed incorrectly. The same override is then compared against `slotStartTime.format(...)` in UTC, which mixes frames. The PR's timezone fix depends on this conversion, so it needs verification with a concrete example (an override near midnight in the organizer zone).

Override timezone conversion depends on an optional field that may be undefined

`override.timeZone` is typed optional in the flattened override (it is set from `availability.timeZone`, which `getUserAvailability` may leave undefined). `dayjs(...).tz(undefined)` then falls back to the local runtime timezone, which differs between server and browser. The computed offset becomes environment dependent. The code should either require the timezone or fall back explicitly to the organizer timezone that `getSlots` already receives. Also, `startTime`/`endTime` are computed as minutes of day only, so an override spanning midnight after the offset shift produces endTime < startTime and is silently dropped by the boundary logic.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag keys: 'shard' vs 'shards'

The produce timer and segment size metrics use the tag `shard`, but the wait_produce timer uses `shards`. Dashboards and alerts filtering on `shard` will miss the wait_produce data, and the same dimension is split across two keys. Use one key consistently.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
--flusher-processes defaults to 1, so the PR's per-shard process model is not the default

The new `--flusher-processes` option defaults to 1. The factory passes this to `SpanFlusher(max_processes=...)`, so with the default every assigned shard is handled by a single flusher process. The PR description says the flusher should spawn a process per redis shard, and the flusher docstring says the same. Production consumers that don't set the flag keep the old single-process throughput, which is the bottleneck this change is meant to remove. The help text 'Defaults to 1' also contradicts the 'one process per shard' behaviour. Either the default should be unset/None (meaning one process per shard) or the description and rollout plan should say the scaling is opt-in.

Added 'hasattr vs isinstance' guidance is unrelated to this PR and misleading

The new 'WRONG: Use hasattr() for unions' example uses `x = 'hello'` with a `str | None` annotation and calls `hasattr(x, 'replace')`. This is not a real union-narrowing bug, and the rule as stated overgeneralises: hasattr is a legitimate duck-typing check. The change also has nothing to do with the span flusher. It should be dropped from this PR or rewritten to describe an actual problem.

Memory info is summed across per-process buffers, which may double-count Redis usage

`submit` now collects `get_memory_info()` from every per-process `SpansBuffer` and sums `used` and `available`. Shards that map to the same redis node (or each buffer reporting the cluster-wide figure) will be counted multiple times, skewing the used/available ratio. The hard-backpressure threshold `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` then trips at the wrong level. Memory info should be de-duplicated per redis node or taken from a single buffer.

New flusher_processes parameter inserted before produce_to_pipe shifts positional arguments

`flusher_processes` was added between `output_block_size` and `produce_to_pipe`. Any existing caller that passes `produce_to_pipe` positionally will now pass it into `flusher_processes`, silently breaking the call. The new parameter should be appended after `produce_to_pipe` or made keyword-only.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code and would restart the wrong thing if used

`_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is never called; `_ensure_processes_alive` restarts by process index. The method also restarts the whole process that owns the shard, which kills the other shards' flushing in that process without going through the kill/restart bookkeeping (`process_restarts`). It should be removed or wired up correctly.

test_basic relies on sleep to wait for a background thread/process

The test adds `time.sleep(0.1)` with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process', then calls `join()`. This is timing-dependent and will be flaky on slow CI, and the test also changes from `django_db` to `transaction=True` without explanation. Synchronize on the flush result (e.g. poll until messages appear with a deadline) instead of a fixed sleep.

test_flusher_processes_limit only checks structure, not that flushing works across processes

The new test asserts the number of processes and shard distribution, but never submits spans or checks that segments from shards handled by the shared process get flushed. The multi-shard-per-process path, which is the new behaviour, is untested for correctness, and restart behaviour is not covered either.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its stated behaviour

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says errors 'don't block offset commits for other messages', but its final assertion is `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, which requires that nothing is committed. Since the failing message is swallowed and offset 101 completes, the implementation commits 102 and this assertion would fail if the test ran to completion. The loop may also exit early, so the test can pass without verifying commit behaviour. The assertion should check that the partition is committed past the failed offset.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
Kafka integration test swallows cleanup errors and uses private StreamProcessor methods

The finally block wraps admin_client.delete_topics in `except Exception: pass`, hiding failures that would leave test topics behind. The test also calls the private processor._run_once() and processor._shutdown(), which are not a stable API. The test is tied to internal Arroyo details and can break on unrelated library updates.

Offset gaps stop commits permanently and the scan is O(range)

get_committable_offsets iterates every integer from start to max_offset and breaks at the first integer that is not in all_offsets (lines 89-93). Kafka offsets are not always contiguous (compacted topics, transaction markers, deleted records). If an offset never appears, the highest committable offset stays stuck at the gap. Committed progress then stops for the life of the process, lag grows, and after a restart the same range is reprocessed. The loop is also proportional to the offset span rather than the number of tracked offsets, so one long-outstanding offset with large offset jumps makes every commit tick (under the partition lock) iterate a huge range.

Queues are unbounded, so the claimed backpressure does not exist

The class docstring of SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but queue.Queue() is created with no maxsize (line 185) and submit() never raises MessageRejected. If the broker delivers faster than the workers process, items accumulate in memory without bound and the consumer never pauses. Either set a maxsize and reject messages when full, or remove the claim.

Strategy close() shuts down the shared FixedQueuePool, which the factory reuses across rebalances

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (and terminate()) call self.queue_pool.shutdown(). The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and passed to every strategy returned by create_thread_queue_parallel_worker. Arroyo creates a new strategy on each partition assignment and closes the old one on rebalance. After the first close, all worker threads exit and the queues are shut down, but the factory still holds the same pool. Any later strategy then calls queue.put() on a shut-down queue, which raises queue.ShutDown. submit() catches that and logs it, so messages are silently dropped and their offsets are marked complete, and the commit thread keeps running against a dead pool. The pool should be owned by the factory (shut down only in factory.shutdown()), or each strategy should own its own pool.

commit_function is called from the commit thread, not the Arroyo processing thread

_commit_loop runs in its own thread and calls self.commit_function(committable), which invokes the Arroyo Commit callable. Arroyo's commit is normally invoked from the strategy's processing thread, and the KafkaConsumer is not documented as thread-safe. Calling it concurrently with the poll loop can corrupt consumer state or raise errors. The commit should be marshalled back to the main thread, for example in poll().

queue.ShutDown only exists on Python 3.13+

queue.ShutDown is referenced in the except clauses of OrderedQueueWorker.run (lines 132 and 142) and in the queue.shutdown() call path. On Python versions before 3.13 the module has no ShutDown attribute. The except expression is evaluated only when an exception is raised, so the worker thread would die with AttributeError as soon as get() or the processing block raises, instead of shutting down cleanly. The repo's supported Python version must be checked, or a sentinel-based shutdown should be used.

shutdown() cannot release a pool that a strategy has already shut down

Because strategies also shut the pool down on close (see queue_consumer.py close()), the factory's shutdown() path and the strategy path both call FixedQueuePool.shutdown() on the same object. The second call is harmless only because shutdown is idempotent in practice. Ownership of the pool should be clarified so that exactly one component shuts it down.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key built by underscore concatenation can collide

userPermDenialCacheKey joins userUID, action, name and parent with '_' without escaping. Folder and dashboard UIDs may contain underscores, so different tuples can produce the same key (for example name "a_b" with parent "" versus name "a" with parent "b"). A collision would deny a request that should be allowed for up to the TTL. Use an unambiguous separator or a hash of the tuple.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache keeps a creator denied on a just-created resource for the full TTL

Check() caches a denial keyed by user, action, name and parent folder for shortCacheTTL (30s) whenever the check is denied (line ~154). The PR's stated purpose is to let a dashboard/folder creator access the resource they just created. If a check for a not-yet-existing resource is denied, the denial is cached. When the resource is created and the permission is granted, the next Check hits the denial cache at line 117 and returns Allowed=false before any permission lookup. Access is therefore still refused for up to 30 seconds, so the reported bug is not fixed. The denial entry is also never invalidated when permissions change. Consider not caching denials for resources that may be newly created, or bypassing the denial cache when the permission set is refreshed.

No test covers the actual regression scenario (deny, then grant, then allow)

TestService_CacheCheck only checks that a pre-seeded denial entry wins over a permission cache entry. It never performs a denied Check, then grants the permission in the store, then checks again and expects Allowed=true. That sequence is the scenario this PR exists for, and the test would have caught the stale denial described above. The test also seeds a permCache value that contradicts the denial, so it does not exercise a realistic cache state.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

GrafanaRuleListItem rendered in list without a React key

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Empty-expression filter runs before interpolation, so a variable that expands to empty is not dropped

The filter `.filter((query) => query.expr)` runs at line 298, before applyTemplateVariables at line 299. A target whose expr is a variable that interpolates to an empty string passes the filter and is sent as an empty query. Filtering after interpolation, or filtering both before and after, would avoid this.

Interpolation before querySupportsSplitting breaks the $__range check

querySupportsSplitting() relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) to keep $__range queries from being split. The comment on that check says the range must not be split because $__range is interpolated on the backend against the split time range. Now that applyTemplateVariables runs at line 299, before partition() at line 300, the expr seen by isQueryWithRangeVariable is already interpolated. If the Loki datasource resolves $__range on the frontend, the variable is gone by the time the check runs, so $__range queries would be split and get an incorrect range. The check should run on the original expression, or the test suite should cover a $__range query to confirm the behaviour is preserved.

Shard path interpolates queries twice, once here and again inside runSplitQuery

runShardSplitQuery() now calls applyTemplateVariables on every target (line 52), and splitQueriesByStreamShard() then builds subRequest with those already-interpolated targets. Each subRequest is passed to runSplitQuery(), which calls applyTemplateVariables again on every target (querySplitting.ts line 299). Interpolation is therefore applied twice to the same expression. Any value that contains a '$' or other template-like text after the first pass gets interpolated a second time. The test change that expects applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times reflects this double application rather than a deliberate design. Interpolation should happen in exactly one place for the sharded path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

Nil request is dereferenced without a guard

QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics read req.PluginContext unconditionally. LoggerMiddleware explicitly guards against a nil req, but this middleware does not. Any caller that passes a nil request into this layer will panic here, which is inconsistent with the rest of the logging chain.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Trace ID no longer appears in the plugin request completion log

logRequest used to add a `traceID` field explicitly via tracing.TraceIDFromContext. That was removed, and the log now relies entirely on m.logger.FromContext(ctx) to carry it. Nothing in this PR adds trace ID to the contextual attributes (instrumentContext only adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname). Unless the infra logger's FromContext happens to include the trace ID, completed-request logs silently lose their trace correlation, which is a regression in observability.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards recorded calls

FromContext returns a brand-new NewTestLogger(), so anything logged through the contextual logger is recorded on a throwaway object. LoggerMiddleware now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so tests that inject TestLogger and assert on InfoLogs will see zero calls and pass or fail for the wrong reason. The fake should return the receiver (or share its log state) so that calls are observed.

false_positives.candidate:
No test covers the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware or the moved logging behavior

The contextual logger logic was moved out of the metrics middleware into a new file, and LoggerMiddleware now depends on it for endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname. None of the tests in this PR verify that ContextualLoggerMiddleware adds these attributes to the context, or that LoggerMiddleware's output still includes them. The existing test still only exercises metrics, with the test name still TestInstrumentationMiddleware.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert (TOCTOU race)

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices and then inserts in a separate statement. Concurrent new anonymous requests can all observe count < deviceLimit and insert, so the limit can be exceeded by the number of concurrent requests. The limit is not enforced under concurrency, which is the core purpose of the feature.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit error now fails the whole anonymous login

Authenticate now returns the ErrDeviceLimitReached error, so once the limit is hit every anonymous request (including ones from already-known devices that go through the update path) is rejected at authentication. Combined with the update path returning the same error for any non-matching row, users may be locked out instead of being served as anonymous without tagging. Confirm this is the intended behavior and that the error does not leak as an unhandled 500.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Limit-reached is signaled via RowsAffected, which is zero when the row is unchanged

updateDevice treats rowsAffected == 0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, RowsAffected returns 0 when the UPDATE sets values identical to existing ones (unless CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS is set), so an existing device re-tagged with the same IP and user agent within the same timestamp window is reported as limit reached and the request is rejected with an error. The error also misidentifies the cause, since a non-matching row (device expired/updated outside window) is also reported as limit reached.

true_positives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count window differs from the window used in the update path and in the API

The limit count uses [now-30d, now+1m] while updateDevice uses [updatedAt-30d, updatedAt+1m] keyed on the device's own timestamp. Both are fine individually, but the count also includes stale rows that the cleanup job has not yet removed (cleanup keeps 61 days), so the count is based on devices updated in the last 30 days only while rows are deleted at 61 days; the semantics of 'device limit' are inconsistent with the stored data. Worth confirming the intended window.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TagDevice now returns DB errors but the caller ignores them for the device-ID path, and the ID-less case still returns nil silently

The new 'return err' in TagDevice is only reached after tagDeviceUI, but tagDeviceUI marks the local cache before the DB write succeeds. If CreateOrUpdateDevice fails (including the limit error), the device key stays in the local cache for 29 minutes, so later requests from that device are skipped without retry and are not tagged, even after space frees up.

false_positives.candidate:
Device limit is read from cfg in the service constructor but the store is no longer injected

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now constructs the store internally with cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit instead of receiving it via Wire. This bypasses dependency injection, makes the store impossible to mock in service-level tests, and the service's anonStore is now a concrete type while the API is passed a.anonStore, so the cleanup/ListDevices behavior cannot be substituted in tests.

Limit test does not cover the update-allowed path or the race

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a second new device is rejected. It does not verify that an existing device can still be updated when the limit is reached, nor that the limit holds under concurrent inserts, nor the API-level behavior of the anonymous client returning an error.

New device_limit setting is undocumented and not validated

The new [auth.anonymous] device_limit key is read with MustInt64(0) but negative values are silently accepted, which the store treats as no limit (>0 check). No documentation or conf/defaults.ini entry is added for the new option, which the PR checklist requires.

Synchronous TagDevice on the request path adds DB latency and removes the timeout

The tagging was previously run in a goroutine with a 2 minute timeout and panic recovery. It is now called synchronously with the request context, so every anonymous authentication performs DB writes (a COUNT plus an insert/update) in the hot path, and the panic recovery was removed. A slow database now slows or fails all anonymous page loads.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine cleanup progress is logged at Error level, including full ID lists, on every batch

In CleanAnnotations (and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags) the normal per-batch progress messages ("Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time", "Tags to clean", "cleaned tags", and the by-count equivalents) are emitted with r.log.Error. Successful routine work is not an error, so this will flood error logs and trip error-based alerting on every cleanup cycle. The ids slice is also logged in full: with batch sizes up to 32767 that is a very large log line per batch. These should be Debug (or Info) and should not dump the ID list. The "err" field is also always nil at the first log call, since err was just checked and returned, so it is misleading.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker interval silently changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

It makes every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history, annotations) run ten times as often, which is a production behaviour change. It looks like a leftover from debugging and should be reverted unless it is intentional and documented.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete attaches the base logger to the context, dropping the name and method fields

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded with the storage metric

In the DeleteCollection goroutine the legacy result is reported via d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...) rather than recordLegacyDuration. Legacy timings and errors are then mixed into the storage metrics.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

Delete records the object name as the kind label in metrics

The storage duration metric on success is called with `name` in the kind position (`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, ...)`), while every other call uses `options.Kind`. This pollutes the metric label cardinality with per-object names and breaks dashboards that group by kind.
