Async legacy Create shares the request object and context with the storage write

Create hands the same `obj` to Storage.Create and then to a goroutine calling Legacy.Create. Storage may mutate that object (e.g. set ResourceVersion, UID, or timestamps) while the goroutine reads it, which is a data race. The goroutine also uses `ctx` from the request; once the HTTP handler returns, the request context is cancelled, so the legacy write can fail or be cut short with the 10s timeout unrelated to the actual work. The legacy copy should get a deep copy of the object and a context detached from request cancellation (e.g. context.WithoutCancel).

Async legacy Update reuses objInfo that storage has already consumed

Update passes the same `objInfo` to Storage.Update and then to Legacy.Update in a goroutine. UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject is typically invoked with the stored old object and may mutate state or be non-reentrant; calling it again concurrently with the storage path is unsafe. The legacy update may also be computed from a different base object than the one storage used, so the two stores can diverge silently. The same request ctx is also reused after the handler returns.

Fire-and-forget legacy writes have no way to surface failures or bound concurrency

All mutating methods launch an unbounded goroutine per request for the legacy write, and failures are only logged as a metric (and the goroutine's log is not used). Under sustained write load goroutines and legacy writes can pile up without limit, and divergence between stores is only visible through metrics. At minimum a bounded worker or queue is needed, and the legacy error should be logged with the object identity.

Mode 3 playlist tests assume legacy writes are synchronous

In mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously, but doPlaylistTests checks the legacy /api/playlists list and per-item legacy GETs immediately after the k8s create/delete calls. These assertions will be flaky or fail whenever the goroutine has not finished, so the new mode 3 integration cases are unreliable. They need to poll/eventually-assert on the legacy side, or the test should check the legacy store only after waiting.

No tests verify the legacy write happens or that legacy failures are ignored

The mode 3 unit tests mock the legacy store with expectations but never assert they were called (no AssertExpectations), and the legacy goroutine may run after the test returns. There is no test that a legacy failure does not change the returned result, and none for the Create/DeleteCollection legacy paths. The core behaviour of mode 3 (sync storage, async legacy) is therefore not actually tested.

Storage failure in Update is recorded as a legacy failure

When Storage.Update returns an error, the code calls recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration. The unified storage error is therefore counted against the legacy store and the storage metric is not updated, making both metrics wrong. Create's storage error path has the same mislabeling issue on the legacy side.

Unrelated checksum entries added to go.work.sum

The go.work.sum change adds many entries for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, otel exporters, etc.) that this feature does not touch. This looks like an accidental tooling side effect and should be dropped from the PR or explained.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No double-check after acquiring the write lock, so cold-start loads repeat

After the RLock fast path misses, the code takes the write lock but does not re-check entryPointAssetsCache. If N requests arrive while the cache is nil (or in Dev mode on every call), each one that acquires the write lock in turn re-reads the manifest from disk or re-fetches it from the CDN, even though the first call has already populated the cache. The fix is to re-read entryPointAssetsCache under the write lock and return early when it is non-nil and cfg.Env != setting.Dev.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
Write lock is held across file I/O and the CDN HTTP request

The exclusive lock is held for the whole duration of readWebAssetsFromCDN (an HTTP GET with only the caller's ctx as a bound) and readWebAssetsFromFile. Until that finishes, every other GetWebAssets caller blocks on RLock, including ones that would otherwise have hit the fast path. A slow or hung CDN therefore stalls all requests that need the page assets. In Dev mode, every request takes the exclusive lock and serializes on disk and network reads. Consider doing the load outside the lock and publishing the result under a short write lock, or at least documenting this trade-off.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions ignores the feature flag and always returns false

The function computes `enabled` from the feature flag but then returns `false` on both branches, so the flag has no effect. Enabling `FlagSqlExpressions` cannot re-enable SQL expressions. This is probably intended as a hard kill switch, but the code reads as if the flag is honored and is misleading. Replace it with an explicit disabled path (or a comment stating the feature is unconditionally off) and remove the dead flag lookup. The `if enabled` check at line 130 also becomes dead logic.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stubbed DB methods break existing SQL command and parser behavior without updated tests

All DB methods now return 'not implemented', so `sql.TablesList` always errors, and `NewSQLCommand`, `SQLCommand.Execute`, and the SQL parsing tests that depend on table extraction will fail. The PR adds no tests for the disabled path, and it does not update or remove the existing SQL tests. Either remove or skip those tests explicitly, or add tests that assert the disabled behavior.

false_positives.candidate:
Error message says 'not implemented' for a feature that is disabled

The user-facing error `sqlExpressions is not implemented` is misleading: SQL expressions are implemented but disabled for security reasons. Users and support staff will be confused about why a previously working query now fails. The message should say the feature is disabled.

Unused stub DB path remains reachable from SQLCommand execution

`UnmarshalSQLCommand` and `Execute` construct commands directly through `sql.NewInMemoryDB()` without going through the reader gate in `reader.go`. The gate is therefore the only protection, and a future caller that uses `NewSQLCommand` directly would bypass the disable check. Put the disable check in `NewSQLCommand` or in the stub layer so it cannot be bypassed.

Variable name `duckDB` no longer refers to DuckDB

After the change `duckDB` holds the stub `*DB`, which has no DuckDB backing. The name is misleading to future readers, and the `TablesList` comment still implies DuckDB-based parsing. Rename the variable and update the comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex lock allows duplicate concurrent builds for the same key

The whole `BuildIndex` used to be serialized by `cacheMu`. The lock now only guards the final map write, so two concurrent `getOrCreateIndex` calls for the same namespace/resource (possible from Search and watch events, which both call `build` when `GetIndex` returns nil) will both build. For file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold) both call `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same directory, and one will fail or corrupt the other. The second build also overwrites the cache entry, leaking the first index. Per-key locking (singleflight or a per-key mutex) is needed, not an unlocked build.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding the lock

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` with no `cacheMu` read lock, while `BuildIndex` writes to the same map under the write lock and `GetIndex` reads it under RLock. Concurrent map iteration and insertion is a fatal runtime error in Go. It is now also called from `searchSupport.init` logging, and `search.init` can run while Search requests are building indexes. It should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Concurrent goroutines write shared `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` during startup indexing

Inside `group.Go(func() error {...})`, the closure assigns to the outer `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments the outer `totalBatchesIndexed` without synchronization. With `initWorkers` > 1 these run concurrently, which is a data race (flagged by `-race`) and can return the wrong error or lose the count. The closure should use a local `err :=` and an atomic counter.

Event broadcaster now starts after the index build, so writes during the build are missed

The order in `Init` was changed so `initWatcher()` runs after `search.init(ctx)`. Any write events that occur while the (now potentially long) index build runs are not buffered by the broadcaster, so Watch clients subscribed through the broadcaster silently miss those events. Previously the watcher was started first to buffer them. The reordering needs justification or the watcher should be started before the build.

Init errors from search build are only logged and the server is left in a half-initialized state on Stop

When `search.init` fails, `initErr` is set and the constructor returns an error, but the search goroutines and lifecycle started earlier (`lifecycle.Init`) are never torn down because `NewResourceServer` returns `nil, err` without calling `Stop`/`cancel`. The background context created in the constructor leaks.

Initialization now runs in the constructor and blocks/fails NewResourceServer

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)`, which runs lifecycle hooks, the full search index build for all namespaces above InitMinCount, and starts the watcher. Callers now get a slow constructor, and any Init failure (including a lifecycle hook that expects the server to be fully constructed or registered) makes the constructor return an error rather than letting the caller handle it. Callers must be audited for whether they can tolerate a long blocking constructor and whether lifecycle hooks depend on the returned server being usable, as the PR asks.

Postgres integration test is now skipped unconditionally

The new skip for `postgres` disables the only integration test covering the storage server target for that database, without any tracking issue beyond a TODO. The change is unrelated to the PR's stated goals and reduces coverage of the lazy-to-eager init change for postgres.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registers removal of a literal "alias" IDP instead of the created alias

In testCacheIDPForLogin the cleanup is registered as `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)`. The string "alias" is a literal, not the IDP alias, so the cleanup attempts to remove an IDP named "alias" that does not exist. The 20 `idp-alias-N` providers created by this test are never removed and leak into the shared test realm, which can change counts in later tests. The same bug appears at line 425 for `idp-alias-20`. The copied pattern in testCacheIDPByOrg (line 303) has the same defect, with an unused `final String alias` variable that was meant to be used.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Search key includes organizationId even for REALM_ONLY, fragmenting the cache

`searchKey` is derived from `organizationId` regardless of `mode`. For REALM_ONLY the result does not depend on organizationId, so callers passing different org ids each produce a separate cached entry (or a cache miss and invalidation via the `cached == null` path) for identical results. The query cache is also rewritten on every such miss, which causes unnecessary churn.

remove() now always loads the IDP from the database

`IdentityProviderModel storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias);` is executed unconditionally. Previously the DB lookup happened only when the alias cache key was invalidated. Every remove now costs an extra DB query, even when the cached entry is available. It is needed for registerIDPLoginInvalidation, but it could reuse the cached IDP for the invalidation of the id and alias keys.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead ASN1Encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder instances and discard the results. They have no effect and only add confusion; the actual encoding is done by the return statement below them.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks every existing CryptoProvider implementation

`int order()` is added as an abstract interface method with no default. Any CryptoProvider implementation that does not implement it (other modules, downstream extensions, test doubles) will fail to compile, and a binary-compatible implementation would throw AbstractMethodError at runtime. A default implementation (for example returning 0) would avoid the break.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Auto-registered provider throws UnsupportedOperationException for most methods

The provider is registered via META-INF/services and has order 100, so it is selected whenever no other provider is on the classpath. Methods such as getKeyStore/getSignature are partially implemented, but getPemUtils, getKeyFactory, getKeyPairGen, getSignature, getCertificateUtils and others throw UnsupportedOperationException. Any authz-client feature that needs them (for example client JWT or signed-token authentication through Http/TokenCallable) will fail at runtime with an unhelpful error rather than a clear configuration message.

CryptoIntegration.init is called on every client creation with a fixed classloader

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now always calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). The init is guarded by a singleton, so the first caller's classloader decides which providers are visible. In a container where the authz client jar is loaded by a different classloader than the application's CryptoProvider, the application's provider is ignored without any warning.

Ignored provider list is passed as a log format string

logger.debugf(builder.toString()) uses the concatenated class-name string as a format pattern. Any '%' in the content would be interpreted as a format specifier and could throw an exception. It should be logger.debugf("%s", builder).

Providers with equal order() are chosen nondeterministically instead of failing

Previously multiple providers on the classpath threw an IllegalStateException. Now they are sorted by order() and the first is silently used. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return 200, so any combination of them (for example Elytron plus Default) resolves by ServiceLoader discovery order, which is not guaranteed. The wrong provider (for example a non-FIPS one in FIPS mode) can then be selected silently. Ties should be rejected or resolved by a deterministic rule.

getKeyStore uses format.name() while the other providers use format.toString()

Other CryptoProvider implementations in this change (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider) call KeyStore.getInstance(format.toString()). If KeystoreFormat overrides toString() with a different keystore type string, this provider will request a different keystore type than the rest of Keycloak.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NPE when the all-clients resource is missing

In hasPermission(ClientModel, scope), if no per-client resource exists, the code loads the 'Clients' type resource via getResourceTypeResource(). That method returns null when the resource is not found. The next line then calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) with a null resource, which can NPE. Even if it doesn't, line 224 uses resource.getScopes() on null. A null check on resource should return false.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Client removal now calls setPermissionsEnabled, which throws in V2

The new ClientRemovedEvent branch calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). When ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is on, management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, and clients() now returns ClientPermissionsV2. Its setPermissionsEnabled() unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException (ClientPermissionsV2 line ~193). Deleting any client in a realm with V2 enabled and this listener active will therefore fail or roll back the deletion. The listener needs to skip or no-op for V2, or ClientPermissionsV2 must implement the cleanup.

canMapRoles and related methods ignore the MANAGE_CLIENTS realm role

canManage(), canConfigure() and canView() all short-circuit when the caller has MANAGE_CLIENTS. canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles and canMapClientScopeRoles only check the schema permission via hasPermission(client, ...). Callers with the manage-clients admin role can therefore be denied role mapping on clients under V2, even though the V1 contract and the interface javadoc treat that role as granting access. Confirm this is intended, and add the role check if not.

requireView() javadoc describes a boolean return instead of a throw

The javadoc for requireView() says 'Returns true if canView() returns true', but the method is void and must throw ForbiddenException when access is denied. The same copy-paste error appears on several other require* methods in this interface, such as requireViewClientScopes. This misleads implementers about the contract.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recreate exit code silently changed from 4 to 3

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE moves from 4 to 3 and FEATURE_DISABLED takes the value 4. Any pipeline or script that already branches on exit code 4 to mean 'recreate upgrade required' will now misread a 'recreate' result as a feature-disabled error, or the reverse. The renumbering is not called out in the PR description. If the command is still considered preview, that should be stated explicitly, or the new code should be introduced without reusing a value that existing consumers depend on.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
Feature-disabled test does not assert the exit code

testFeatureNotEnabled only checks the error message. The new behaviour's key contract, documented in update-compatibility.adoc as exit code 4, is never verified, so a regression in the exit code (for example the renumbering above) would go unnoticed for the metadata and check commands.

setEnabledFeatures overwrites any features already configured on the test deployment

createInitialDeployment calls setEnabledFeatures(List.of(ROLLING_UPDATES)) on the FeatureSpec, replacing whatever enabled features getTestKeycloakDeployment() configured. If the base deployment enables other features, the tests silently lose them. The code should append to the existing list instead of replacing it.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses group resource name as group id but resources are named by id only in V2

In V2 the group-type resource is looked up by type and the callback adds groupResource.getId() (a resource UUID) to the granted set, while callers use the set as group IDs for the user search filter. Resource IDs are internal store IDs, not group IDs, so the returned set does not match group IDs and the group-membership based user filtering in UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource silently returns wrong results. Resource name (group id) should be used instead.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

false_positives.candidate:
Group removal listener is now only registered under the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature check at registration time

registerListener now checks the feature flag once when registering and no longer per event; if the feature flag state changes at runtime or differs between registration and dispatch, behaviour changes. More importantly the listener is now skipped entirely when the flag is off, which is the intended behaviour, but the change is unrelated to the PR's stated scope and untested.

GroupPermissionsV2 overrides throw UnsupportedOperationException for methods still reachable from V2 code paths

isPermissionsEnabled and setPermissionsEnabled throw in V2, but GroupResource.getManagementPermissions/setManagementPermissionsEnabled call AdminPermissions.management(...).groups().isPermissionsEnabled() and setPermissionsEnabled() on V2 when the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature is enabled, so these REST endpoints now throw 500 instead of returning a meaningful response.

Javadoc for canManage/canView/canManageGroupMembership mentions group-chain permissions the implementation does not check for every method

The javadoc for canMapRoles and canManageGroupMembership claims MANAGE_MEMBERS of the group chain grants access, and canImpersonate docs are inconsistent with code; docs and behaviour diverge, misleading integrators.

Test class has stray double semicolon and no negative test for group membership view via users endpoint

The field declaration ends with ';;' and the view-members test only checks positive visibility; there is no test asserting that a user outside the group stays hidden when only VIEW on Groups is granted, which is the core security property of the new Groups resource type.

canManage() replaced default check with hasOneAdminRole, dropping V2 permission-based fallback semantics

GroupPermissions.canManage() now only checks MANAGE_USERS role, while the removed canManageDefault delegated to the users permission evaluator. Callers relying on canManage() for the realm-level grant no longer get consistent behaviour with UserPermissions.canManage(), which uses the same role check but the base class is also used for V1 where permission-based realm-level manage was previously evaluated via users().

canMapRoles and canManageGroupMembership now fall back to group-based management without restoring the removed MANAGE check

canMapRoles/canManageGroupMembership in V2 now grant access via canManageByGroup (MANAGE_MEMBERS on a group), which broadens the permission model beyond what the schema documents for MAP_ROLES/MANAGE_GROUP_MEMBERSHIP; this is an unintended authorization expansion relative to the stated scopes and is not covered by tests for the negative case.

hasPermission looks up group resource by name but uses null-group fallback wrongly for canView/canManage without group

hasPermission(null, ...) falls back to the all-groups resource and checks policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) with a resource that may be null if the Groups type resource does not exist, causing a NullPointerException rather than a denial when the resource type resource is missing.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).

Lithuanian account message replaced with Italian text

totpStep1 in the Lithuanian account bundle is now 'Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:', which is Italian. Lithuanian users will see Italian in the TOTP setup page. The original Lithuanian translation was removed to satisfy the sanitizer rather than fixing the markup.

true_positives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Anchor replacement removes first occurrence anywhere, not at the matched position

santizeAnchors uses value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "") which strips the first textual occurrence of the anchor tag, not the one the matcher found. With repeated identical anchors, or when the translation has an anchor text that appears earlier in a different position, the wrong tag is removed and the comparison against the English tag list becomes inconsistent. Also the English matcher is advanced in lockstep with no check that the number of anchors matches, so a translation with fewer anchors passes silently.

true_positives.golden_comment: Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Policy and pattern fields are package-visible instance fields

POLICY_SOME_HTML, POLICY_NO_HTML and HTML_TAGS are non-private, non-static instance fields rebuilt per object. They should be static final constants; the policy factory is relatively expensive to construct and is needlessly recreated for every file verified.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').

false_positives.candidate:
Admin UI message uses MessageFormat placeholders while the admin UI uses i18next double braces

error-invalid-multivalued-size is changed to {0} / {2,choice,...} syntax, but this admin-ui bundle is consumed by i18next which expects {{0}}. Users will see raw placeholders and choice markup in the admin console.

Admin theme message switched to MessageFormat choice syntax without matching renderer

error-invalid-multivalued-size now uses {2,choice,...} syntax. Other admin messages in this file use plain {n} placeholders consumed by the admin UI; if that UI does not run MessageFormat choice evaluation, users will see literal choice markup.

Bulk whitespace-only edits across many locale files Dozens of login messages only change '
' to '

The account UI is a React/i18next app which interpolates {{...}} and does not evaluate MessageFormat choice syntax, so the rendered message will show the raw '{0}' and '{2,choice,...}' text to users.

Czech multivalued-size choice format has inconsistent plural forms

error-invalid-multivalued-size in Czech uses choice patterns '0#hodnot|1#hodnotu|1<hodnoty|4<hodnot' which is inconsistent with the other locales and with the English pattern; the value 1 uses 'hodnotu' correctly but the 2-4 case relies on the '1<hodnoty' rule with a '4<' boundary that drops the 2-4 distinction incorrectly.

Dutch emailVerificationBodyHtml unbalanced tag change The change closes a

with '' typo fixed to '

' which is correct, but the associated diff indicates a broken closing tag was in the original; no validation was added to the verifier to catch this class of error, so the fix relies on manual edits across 40+ files.

The English counterpart path is computed by regex replacing '_[a-zA-Z-_]*\.properties' with '_en.properties' on the whole absolute path. Any '_' in parent directories (e.g. a checkout path like /home/user/my_repo/...) is not affected since the regex requires '.properties' suffix, but the file-name pattern is applied greedily from the first underscore-containing segment of the filename only; more importantly for files like 'messages_zh_CN.properties' it works, yet for the theme-verifier fixtures (e.g. 'noHtml_de.properties' -> 'noHtml_en.properties') it is fine. Also if the English file does not exist the code throws RuntimeException, aborting the whole verification instead of reporting a message, which crashes the Maven build for any locale file lacking an English counterpart.

Fixture is unclosed HTML and the test does not verify it is the English file being checked

illegalHtmlTag_en.properties contains '<div>tag</div' (missing '>'), which is a malformed tag rather than a clearly illegal one; the test name suggests an illegal tag but the fixture tests a broken closing tag. All mutating methods launch an unbounded goroutine per request for the legacy write, and failures are only logged as a metric (and the goroutine's log is not used). true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is not atomic, allowing replay

The code checks the backup code index, then later writes back the re-encrypted array with the used code nulled, in a separate non-transactional update. Two concurrent login requests with the same valid backup code can both pass the indexOf check before either write lands, so one backup code can be used twice. The code is single-use by design, so this breaks the security guarantee.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue describe the exact same race condition: backup codes are checked and updated in memory before being written back without atomicity/transactions, allowing concurrent login requests to reuse a single-use backup code.

false_positives.candidate:
Used backup code is set to null, but indexOf of a null entry and remaining codes are not validated

Setting backupCodes[index] = null keeps the array length, and the stored JSON contains nulls. Submitting an empty or whitespace string after replaceAll can match a null entry only if the input is null, which is not possible from a string, so this is mostly safe, but a user submitting an input that is the empty string bypasses the check because credentials.backupCode is falsy and falls back to TOTP. More concretely, the truthiness check on backupCode means an attacker-supplied backupCode of an empty string skips backup verification entirely; the backup-code path is only reached when the field is non-empty.

Backup code verification is not consumed and the disable path accepts an unvalidated body value

req.body.backupCode.replaceAll is called on a value that may not be a string (JSON body can send a number or object), which throws a 500 instead of a clean error. Also the used backup code is never consumed here, but the subsequent update wipes all backup codes anyway, so this is acceptable only if disabling is the sole consumer; the reliance on the later update is implicit and fragile.

JSON.parse of decrypted backup codes can throw unhandled

If the stored backupCodes is corrupted or the decryption key changed, symmetricDecrypt or JSON.parse throws, producing an unhandled exception and a 500 with no ErrorCode. The same unguarded parse exists in next-auth-options.ts authorize, where it aborts login with an unmapped error.

Setup overwrites existing backup codes before enable, invalidating the previous set on abandoned setup

Backup codes are written to the DB at setup time while twoFactorEnabled is still false. If the user abandons enrollment, the previously stored codes are replaced anyway, and the codes shown to the user are only persisted, not confirmed. Also, codes are generated even if the user never completes the TOTP step, so the displayed codes can be out of sync with what is stored if setup is called twice (the second call overwrites the first set the user may have already saved).

backupCodes state typed as untyped empty array

useState([]) infers never[] under strict typing and the later assignment from body.backupCodes is untyped (any), weakening type safety for the displayed and downloaded codes.

Blob URL created on every setup call but revoked only against stale state

backupCodesUrl is read from closure state inside handleSetup, so if the user retries setup in the same render cycle the revoke may target a stale URL and leak or revoke the wrong object URL. The download link may then point to a revoked URL.

Backup code errors are shown via next-auth result but the error message path for SecondFactorRequired still relies on ErrorCode mapping that drops IncorrectBackupCode in errorMessages

The new branches set error text directly, but the Lost access flow never resets twoFactorRequired on credential errors, and when a backup code is wrong the TwoFactor totp input is not shown, so the user cannot see the field they must fix. The error message localization keys are also added only to en/common.json, so other locales fall back to raw keys.

No test covers backup code login, the core feature of this PR

The only tests exercise TOTP enable and disable plus backup download UI. Nothing verifies that a backup code logs in, that a used code is rejected on reuse, or that a wrong code shows the new error. The TODO acknowledges this, yet the PR checklist claims no tests were added.

Backup codes stored as encrypted blob in plain TEXT column without versioning

The codes are JSON encrypted with the global CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY. Rotating the key makes all stored backup codes unreadable, and the authorize and disable paths throw an internal error rather than prompting regeneration. No migration path or key rotation handling is provided.

Unrelated tabIndex change on password visibility toggle

Adding tabIndex={-1} to the show/hide password button in the shared PasswordField removes it from keyboard tab order across the whole app, an accessibility regression unrelated to backup codes and not described in the PR.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach with async callback discards promises; deletions run unawaited and errors become unhandled rejections

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` does not await the async callbacks, so the surrounding try/catch never catches errors from getCalendar or deleteEvent. Those rejections become unhandled promise rejections, and the reschedule returns before calendar cleanup finishes. The same pattern is repeated in wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts, trpc bookings.tsx, and handleCancelBooking.ts (recurring branch).
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: using `forEach` with an `async` callback causes the promises to run unawaited, bypassing surrounding `try/catch` blocks, causing unhandled promise rejections, and leading to incomplete cleanup before the function returns.

false_positives.candidate:
appStore entries are now unresolved Promises, but callers still use them synchronously in places

The appStore object now maps each key to a dynamic import() Promise instead of a module namespace. Any consumer that accesses `appStore[x].lib` (or `"lib" in appStore[x]`) without awaiting gets a Promise, so the `"lib" in app` check is always false and the feature silently behaves as unimplemented. Call sites not updated in this PR (e.g. other usages across the repo beyond the 12 files, such as getApps/utils or payment/locations code that reads appStore synchronously) will break silently rather than fail loudly.

Mapping to import() promises changes the module type contract for all importers

Previously the default export was a map of module namespaces; now every property is Promise<module>. Any type-level consumer expecting the namespace shape will fail type checking or, if using `as`/casts, fail at runtime. The PR does not show a single shared type or helper (e.g. a typed async accessor) to enforce awaiting, so future callers will easily make the same mistake.

getCalendarCredentials calls async getCalendar without awaiting, yielding Promise objects as calendars

getCalendar is now async, but getCalendarCredentials still does `const calendar = getCalendar(credential);` and stores the Promise in the returned object. Downstream code in getConnectedCalendars then does `await item.calendar`, which works only by accident, but any other consumer of getCalendarCredentials reading `.calendar` synchronously will get a Promise and treat it as a non-null Calendar, calling methods on it and failing.

Recurring-cancel calendar deletions run in an un-awaited forEach async callback

`.forEach(async (credential) => { ... await calendar?.deleteEvent ... apiDeletes.push(...) })` pushes into apiDeletes after `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` has already captured the array, so these deletions are neither awaited nor have their errors surfaced; the booking can be reported cancelled while calendar events remain, and rejections are unhandled.

getVideoAdapters now awaits each app sequentially, serializing imports

updateMeeting does not handle getVideoAdapters failure; createMeeting error path also changed

await used inside a non-async callback context

Payment app lookup returns null from a mutation path after a warn, but the function signature expects a result

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag keys: 'shard' vs 'shards'

The produce timer and segment size metrics use the tag `shard`, but the wait_produce timer uses `shards`. Dashboards and alerts filtering on `shard` will miss the wait_produce data, and the same dimension is split across two keys. Use one key consistently.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same inconsistent 'shard' versus 'shards' metric tag keys across produce, segment size, and wait_produce metrics, including the resulting aggregation and dashboard filtering problems.

false_positives.candidate:
--flusher-processes defaults to 1, so the PR's per-shard process model is not the default

The new `--flusher-processes` option defaults to 1. The factory passes this to `SpanFlusher(max_processes=...)`, so with the default every assigned shard is handled by a single flusher process. The PR description says the flusher should spawn a process per redis shard, and the flusher docstring says the same. Production consumers that don't set the flag keep the old single-process throughput, which is the bottleneck this change is meant to remove. The help text 'Defaults to 1' also contradicts the 'one process per shard' behaviour. Either the default should be unset/None (meaning one process per shard) or the description and rollout plan should say the scaling is opt-in.

New flusher_processes parameter inserted before produce_to_pipe shifts positional arguments

`flusher_processes` was added between `output_block_size` and `produce_to_pipe`. Any existing caller that passes `produce_to_pipe` positionally will now pass it into `flusher_processes`, silently breaking the call. The new parameter should be appended after `produce_to_pipe` or made keyword-only.

_create_process_for_shard is dead code and would restart the wrong thing if used

`_create_process_for_shard` (singular) is never called; `_ensure_processes_alive` restarts by process index. The method also restarts the whole process that owns the shard, which kills the other shards' flushing in that process without going through the kill/restart bookkeeping (`process_restarts`). It should be removed or wired up correctly.

Memory info is summed across per-process buffers, which may double-count Redis usage

`submit` now collects `get_memory_info()` from every per-process `SpansBuffer` and sums `used` and `available`. Shards that map to the same redis node (or each buffer reporting the cluster-wide figure) will be counted multiple times, skewing the used/available ratio. The hard-backpressure threshold `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` then trips at the wrong level. Memory info should be de-duplicated per redis node or taken from a single buffer.

test_basic relies on sleep to wait for a background thread/process

The test adds `time.sleep(0.1)` with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process', then calls `join()`. This is timing-dependent and will be flaky on slow CI, and the test also changes from `django_db` to `transaction=True` without explanation. Synchronize on the flush result (e.g. poll until messages appear with a deadline) instead of a fixed sleep.

test_flusher_processes_limit only checks structure, not that flushing works across processes

The new test asserts the number of processes and shard distribution, but never submits spans or checks that segments from shards handled by the shared process get flushed. The multi-shard-per-process path, which is the new behaviour, is untested for correctness, and restart behaviour is not covered either.

Added 'hasattr vs isinstance' guidance is unrelated to this PR and misleading

The new 'WRONG: Use hasattr() for unions' example uses `x = 'hello'` with a `str | None` annotation and calls `hasattr(x, 'replace')`. This is not a real union-narrowing bug, and the rule as stated overgeneralises: hasattr is a legitimate duck-typing check. The change also has nothing to do with the span flusher. It should be dropped from this PR or rewritten to describe an actual problem.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

Removing the BuildIndex lock allows duplicate concurrent builds for the same key

The whole `BuildIndex` used to be serialized by `cacheMu`. The lock now only guards the final map write, so two concurrent `getOrCreateIndex` calls for the same namespace/resource (possible from Search and watch events, which both call `build` when `GetIndex` returns nil) will both build. For file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold) both call `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same directory, and one will fail or corrupt the other. The second build also overwrites the cache entry, leaking the first index. Per-key locking (singleflight or a per-key mutex) is needed, not an unlocked build.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: narrowing cacheMu protection to the final cache assignment allows concurrent BuildIndex calls to redundantly build the same index for the same key. The candidate's additional consequences and proposed fix do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` with no `cacheMu` read lock, while `BuildIndex` writes to the same map under the write lock and `GetIndex` reads it under RLock. Concurrent map iteration and insertion is a fatal runtime error in Go. It is now also called from `searchSupport.init` logging, and `search.init` can run while Search requests are building indexes. It should take `cacheMu.RLock()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unsynchronized iteration of b.cache in TotalDocs racing with BuildIndex writes, potentially causing a concurrent map iteration/write panic. The candidate describes a different concurrency trigger but matches the underlying bug and affected call.

false_positives.candidate:

Inside `group.Go(func() error {...})`, the closure assigns to the outer `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments the outer `totalBatchesIndexed` without synchronization. With `initWorkers` > 1 these run concurrently, which is a data race (flagged by `-race`) and can return the wrong error or lose the count. The closure should use a local `err :=` and an atomic counter.

Initialization now runs in the constructor and blocks/fails NewResourceServer

`NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)`, which runs lifecycle hooks, the full search index build for all namespaces above InitMinCount, and starts the watcher. Callers now get a slow constructor, and any Init failure (including a lifecycle hook that expects the server to be fully constructed or registered) makes the constructor return an error rather than letting the caller handle it. Callers must be audited for whether they can tolerate a long blocking constructor and whether lifecycle hooks depend on the returned server being usable, as the PR asks.

Event broadcaster now starts after the index build, so writes during the build are missed

The order in `Init` was changed so `initWatcher()` runs after `search.init(ctx)`. Any write events that occur while the (now potentially long) index build runs are not buffered by the broadcaster, so Watch clients subscribed through the broadcaster silently miss those events. Previously the watcher was started first to buffer them. The reordering needs justification or the watcher should be started before the build.

Init errors from search build are only logged and the server is left in a half-initialized state on Stop

When `search.init` fails, `initErr` is set and the constructor returns an error, but the search goroutines and lifecycle started earlier (`lifecycle.Init`) are never torn down because `NewResourceServer` returns `nil, err` without calling `Stop`/`cancel`. The background context created in the constructor leaks.

The new skip for `postgres` disables the only integration test covering the storage server target for that database, without any tracking issue beyond a TODO. The change is unrelated to the PR's stated goals and reduces coverage of the lazy-to-eager init change for postgres.

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close() shuts down the shared FixedQueuePool, which the factory reuses across rebalances

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (and terminate()) call self.queue_pool.shutdown(). The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and passed to every strategy returned by create_thread_queue_parallel_worker. Arroyo creates a new strategy on each partition assignment and closes the old one on rebalance. After the first close, all worker threads exit and the queues are shut down, but the factory still holds the same pool. Any later strategy then calls queue.put() on a shut-down queue, which raises queue.ShutDown. submit() catches that and logs it, so messages are silently dropped and their offsets are marked complete, and the commit thread keeps running against a dead pool. The pool should be owned by the factory (shut down only in factory.shutdown()), or each strategy should own its own pool.

queue.ShutDown only exists on Python 3.13+

queue.ShutDown is referenced in the except clauses of OrderedQueueWorker.run (lines 132 and 142) and in the queue.shutdown() call path. On Python versions before 3.13 the module has no ShutDown attribute. The except expression is evaluated only when an exception is raised, so the worker thread would die with AttributeError as soon as get() or the processing block raises, instead of shutting down cleanly. The repo's supported Python version must be checked, or a sentinel-based shutdown should be used.

Queues are unbounded, so the claimed backpressure does not exist

The class docstring of SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but queue.Queue() is created with no maxsize (line 185) and submit() never raises MessageRejected. If the broker delivers faster than the workers process, items accumulate in memory without bound and the consumer never pauses. Either set a maxsize and reject messages when full, or remove the claim.

Offset gaps stop commits permanently and the scan is O(range)

get_committable_offsets iterates every integer from start to max_offset and breaks at the first integer that is not in all_offsets (lines 89-93). Kafka offsets are not always contiguous (compacted topics, transaction markers, deleted records). If an offset never appears, the highest committable offset stays stuck at the gap. Committed progress then stops for the life of the process, lag grows, and after a restart the same range is reprocessed. The loop is also proportional to the offset span rather than the number of tracked offsets, so one long-outstanding offset with large offset jumps makes every commit tick (under the partition lock) iterate a huge range.

commit_function is called from the commit thread, not the Arroyo processing thread

_commit_loop runs in its own thread and calls self.commit_function(committable), which invokes the Arroyo Commit callable. Arroyo's commit is normally invoked from the strategy's processing thread, and the KafkaConsumer is not documented as thread-safe. Calling it concurrently with the poll loop can corrupt consumer state or raise errors. The commit should be marshalled back to the main thread, for example in poll().

shutdown() cannot release a pool that a strategy has already shut down

Because strategies also shut the pool down on close (see queue_consumer.py close()), the factory's shutdown() path and the strategy path both call FixedQueuePool.shutdown() on the same object. The second call is harmless only because shutdown is idempotent in practice. Ownership of the pool should be clarified so that exactly one component shuts it down.

Kafka integration test swallows cleanup errors and uses private StreamProcessor methods

The finally block wraps admin_client.delete_topics in `except Exception: pass`, hiding failures that would leave test topics behind. The test also calls the private processor._run_once() and processor._shutdown(), which are not a stable API. The test is tied to internal Arroyo details and can break on unrelated library updates.

false_positives.candidate:
Span-count cap removed from Python side while Lua now trims to 1000 silently

The max_segment_spans check was removed from _load_segment_data, so oversized segments are no longer skipped and logged. Meanwhile the Lua script now silently zpopmin-trims sets to 1000 entries, dropping spans without any metric or log. Segments with more spans than the limit lose data silently and the max_segment_spans parameter is now dead code.

zpopmin trims the lowest-scored (oldest) spans, not the excess

zpopmin removes the members with the smallest scores, so when the set exceeds 1000 spans the oldest spans are discarded. This is the opposite of what is probably desired for a bounded buffer and also the span_count used is from zunionstore which returns the union cardinality, so the trim count is computed correctly but the chosen eviction policy silently drops data from the start of the segment.

zunionstore with weights defaults sums scores; spans re-added with same payload are merged incorrectly

zunionstore uses the default AGGREGATE SUM, so when the same payload member exists in both sets its score is summed instead of kept. Since members are the raw payload and scores are end timestamps, duplicate spans moved between sets get their timestamp doubled, corrupting eviction ordering.

Span payload timestamp used as sort score makes ZADD of duplicate payloads ineffective

process_spans builds a dict {payload: end_timestamp} for zadd; if two identical payloads occur in a batch the dict dedupes them, which is fine, but the pipeline previously used sadd. Score-based sets also change the flush_segments/_load_segment_data contract (zscan returns (member, score) tuples) without any migration for segments already stored as Redis sets, causing WRONGTYPE errors on rolling deploy.

Advanced pagination gated by query parameter and privilege without tests

The optimized paginator is enabled by a client-supplied query parameter for superusers or global-access members, and the endpoint now differs in pagination behavior. There is no test covering this branch, and the 'enable_advanced' flag unlocks the negative-offset path in the paginator, expanding what an admin request can read in audit logs.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. The cache key embeds hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))). Python's hash() for ints is stable, but the key is also not tied to the allowlist value; more importantly the cache stores only the boolean eligibility per project set for 60s, so an allowlist change is ignored for up to 60 seconds while the code comment claims this is safe. invalidate_upsampling_cache is defined but never called, so the advertised invalidation on allowlist change does not happen. Cache hit short-circuits on falsy check incorrectly typed; cache.get returns non-bool values

If the cached value is False, the function returns False, which is correct, but the return type is not guaranteed to be bool when cached_result is a non-bool stored by another writer under the same key. Membership test is O(n*m) on a list read from options

`project_id in allowlist` performs a linear scan of the allowlist for each project, and the allowlist is a list from options. For large allowlists and many projects this is quadratic per request. Converting to a set once would be the expected approach given the stated performance goal.

The comment asserts the schema guarantees the column for all events, but the endpoint does not verify this beyond the allowlist check. The result also silently changes the metric name the user requested (count() is returned aliased as count), which can break clients that expect the column type.

Folder and dashboard UIDs may contain underscores, so different tuples can produce the same key (for example name "a_b" with parent "" versus name "a" with parent "b"). The PR's stated purpose is to let a dashboard/folder creator access the resource they just created. If a check for a not-yet-existing resource is denied, the denial is cached. When the resource is created and the permission is granted, the next Check hits the denial cache at line 117 and returns Allowed=false before any permission lookup. Access is therefore still refused for up to 30 seconds, so the reported bug is not fixed. The denial entry is also never invalidated when permissions change. The test also seeds a permCache value that contradicts the denial, so it does not exercise a realistic cache state.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No double-check after acquiring the write lock, so cold-start loads repeat

After the RLock fast path misses, the code takes the write lock but does not re-check entryPointAssetsCache. If N requests arrive while the cache is nil (or in Dev mode on every call), each one that acquires the write lock in turn re-reads the manifest from disk or re-fetches it from the CDN, even though the first call has already populated the cache. The fix is to re-read entryPointAssetsCache under the write lock and return early when it is non-nil and cfg.Env != setting.Dev.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock, allowing concurrent callers that missed the read-lock fast path to redundantly populate an already-filled cache.

false_positives.candidate:
Write lock is held across file I/O and the CDN HTTP request

The exclusive lock is held for the whole duration of readWebAssetsFromCDN (an HTTP GET with only the caller's ctx as a bound) and readWebAssetsFromFile. Until that finishes, every other GetWebAssets caller blocks on RLock, including ones that would otherwise have hit the fast path. A slow or hung CDN therefore stalls all requests that need the page assets. In Dev mode, every request takes the exclusive lock and serializes on disk and network reads. Consider doing the load outside the lock and publishing the result under a short write lock, or at least documenting this trade-off.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

The "err" field is also always nil at the first log call, since err was just checked and returned, so it is misleading.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records the object name as the kind label in metrics

The storage duration metric on success is called with `name` in the kind position (`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, ...)`), while every other call uses `options.Kind`. This pollutes the metric label cardinality with per-object names and breaks dashboards that group by kind.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same inconsistency: Delete passes the object name instead of options.Kind as the kind label when recording storage duration metrics.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy Create shares the request object and context with the storage write

Create hands the same `obj` to Storage.Create and then to a goroutine calling Legacy.Create. Storage may mutate that object (e.g. set ResourceVersion, UID, or timestamps) while the goroutine reads it, which is a data race. The goroutine also uses `ctx` from the request; once the HTTP handler returns, the request context is cancelled, so the legacy write can fail or be cut short with the 10s timeout unrelated to the actual work. The legacy copy should get a deep copy of the object and a context detached from request cancellation (e.g. context.WithoutCancel).

Async legacy Update reuses objInfo that storage has already consumed

Update passes the same `objInfo` to Storage.Update and then to Legacy.Update in a goroutine. UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject is typically invoked with the stored old object and may mutate state or be non-reentrant; calling it again concurrently with the storage path is unsafe. The legacy update may also be computed from a different base object than the one storage used, so the two stores can diverge silently. The same request ctx is also reused after the handler returns.

Storage failure in Update is recorded as a legacy failure

When Storage.Update returns an error, the code calls recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of recordStorageDuration. The unified storage error is therefore counted against the legacy store and the storage metric is not updated, making both metrics wrong. Create's storage error path has the same mislabeling issue on the legacy side.

Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded with the storage metric

In the DeleteCollection goroutine the legacy result is reported via d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...) rather than recordLegacyDuration. Legacy timings and errors are then mixed into the storage metrics.

Fire-and-forget legacy writes have no way to surface failures or bound concurrency

All mutating methods launch an unbounded goroutine per request for the legacy write, and failures are only logged as a metric (and the goroutine's log is not used). Under sustained write load goroutines and legacy writes can pile up without limit, and divergence between stores is only visible through metrics. At minimum a bounded worker or queue is needed, and the legacy error should be logged with the object identity.

Mode 3 playlist tests assume legacy writes are synchronous

In mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously, but doPlaylistTests checks the legacy /api/playlists list and per-item legacy GETs immediately after the k8s create/delete calls. These assertions will be flaky or fail whenever the goroutine has not finished, so the new mode 3 integration cases are unreliable. They need to poll/eventually-assert on the legacy side, or the test should check the legacy store only after waiting.

No tests verify the legacy write happens or that legacy failures are ignored

The mode 3 unit tests mock the legacy store with expectations but never assert they were called (no AssertExpectations), and the legacy goroutine may run after the test returns. There is no test that a legacy failure does not change the returned result, and none for the Create/DeleteCollection legacy paths. The core behaviour of mode 3 (sync storage, async legacy) is therefore not actually tested.

The go.work.sum change adds many entries for unrelated modules (grafana-azure-sdk-go, prometheus-alertmanager, otel exporters, etc.) that this feature does not touch. This looks like an accidental tooling side effect and should be dropped from the PR or explained.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check rejects any slot that falls outside any single working-hours range

The working-hours guard uses `workingHours.find(...)` and returns false if the callback is truthy. The callback is truthy whenever one particular range does not contain the slot. So for a day with several ranges (for example 9-12 and 14-18, or aggregated hours from multiple hosts), a slot inside one range is rejected because it is outside another. The intended semantics is 'outside all ranges', which needs `every`/`some` logic. Also `end` is computed from `slotStartTime` instead of the slot end, so `end > workingHour.endTime` checks the start, not the end. Finally, the comparison uses UTC day and hour while `WorkingHours` values are minutes in the organizer timezone (per the type doc), so the check is evaluated in the wrong timezone. This is a regression that can remove valid slots for any multi-range or cross-timezone schedule.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that `end` is computed from `slotStartTime` instead of the slot end, matching the golden issue, even though it also discusses other bugs.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Comparing dayjs objects with === is always false

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares object identity, not time. The branch that treats a zero-length override as a special case never runs. Use `.isSame(...)` or compare `valueOf()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify strict equality between dayjs objects as comparing object references rather than date values, and recommend .isSame() to fix the comparison.

false_positives.candidate:
Date override logic accepts partially overlapping slots and rejects slots when several overrides share a day

`dateOverrideExist` is set true for any override on the same day, and `find` returns true (meaning 'reject') as soon as any override on that day does not contain the slot. Consequences: (1) with two overrides on the same day, a slot inside override A is rejected because it is outside override B. (2) A slot that starts before an override's start and ends after it (partial overlap) matches none of the rejection conditions. It falls through to `return true` and is accepted even though it is not fully inside the override. The containment test must be: slot start >= override start and slot end <= override end, evaluated across all overrides for the day, with a clear rule for when no override covers the slot.

Organizer timezone offset sign looks inverted for override conversion

`utcOffset = dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1` negates the organizer's offset. For Asia/Kolkata (+330) this shifts the override by -330 minutes, so the local day of the override is computed incorrectly. The same override is then compared against `slotStartTime.format(...)` in UTC, which mixes frames. The PR's timezone fix depends on this conversion, so it needs verification with a concrete example (an override near midnight in the organizer zone).

Override timezone conversion depends on an optional field that may be undefined

`override.timeZone` is typed optional in the flattened override (it is set from `availability.timeZone`, which `getUserAvailability` may leave undefined). `dayjs(...).tz(undefined)` then falls back to the local runtime timezone, which differs between server and browser. The computed offset becomes environment dependent. The code should either require the timezone or fall back explicitly to the organizer timezone that `getSlots` already receives. Also, `startTime`/`endTime` are computed as minutes of day only, so an override spanning midnight after the offset shift produces endTime < startTime and is silently dropped by the boundary logic.

New timezone test does not exercise the bug it claims to cover

The added test asserts that the same UTC slots are returned for the attendee timezone +6:00 as for +5:30. It reuses the existing expectation, so it passes whether or not overrides are adjusted correctly. It does not cover the reported case: an organizer override whose organizer timezone differs from the schedule timezone, where the attendee's timezone should change which slots appear. No test covers the round-robin fixed-host override fix either, which is the primary change in the description.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry increment uses a stale in-memory value instead of an atomic increment

`retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` writes a value read earlier in the run. If another worker or run updates the same row concurrently, one increment can be lost, so the row may survive longer than the intended two-failure limit. Prisma's `{ increment: 1 }` would avoid this.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 uses a potentially stale value, causing lost increments under concurrency, and recommend Prisma's atomic increment. The candidate matches the underlying issue despite not explicitly mentioning the catch block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount cleanup deletes reminders of every method, not just SMS

The second branch of the deleteMany OR (`retryCount: { gt: 1 }`) has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` constraint, unlike the first branch. Any WorkflowReminder row with retryCount > 1, including EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders that this SMS cron never touches, will be hard-deleted on every run. The condition should be scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` as well.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing WorkflowMethods.SMS filter in the retryCount > 1 deletion branch, which incorrectly deletes non-SMS reminders such as Email and WhatsApp.

false_positives.candidate:
Unguarded DB update in catch block can abort the whole cron run

The new `prisma.workflowReminder.update` inside the catch block is not wrapped in its own try/catch. If it throws (for example the row was deleted by a concurrent run), the exception escapes the for-loop and every remaining unscheduled reminder in the batch is skipped, and the handler returns an error instead of `SMS scheduled`.

Reminders with missing workflowStep/booking or empty message never accrue retries

When `!reminder.workflowStep || !reminder.booking` the loop `continue`s without incrementing retryCount, and when the message is empty or sendTo is missing the `if (message?.length ...)` block is skipped, so no retry is recorded. Such rows stay unscheduled and are never cleaned up by the new retry-based deletion, so they are retried indefinitely on every cron run, which is the behavior this PR is meant to stop.

Public findMany() removed and replaced by getBaseConditions() without updating callers

The `findMany` method was removed and replaced by `getBaseConditions()`, which returns only a raw `Prisma.Sql` fragment. Any existing caller of `InsightsBookingService.findMany(...)` will fail to compile or break at runtime, and callers that relied on Prisma `select`/`where` arguments have no equivalent. The PR does not show any caller migration, so this is a breaking API change hidden inside a test-focused PR. Callers need to be found and migrated, or the change should be called out explicitly.

Caching tests deleted with no replacement

The `Caching` describe block (verifying that getAuthorizationConditions and getFilterConditions return memoized results on the second call) was removed entirely, and the PR description does not mention it. The service still implements memoization via cachedAuthConditions/cachedFilterConditions, so that behavior is now untested.

PR description says the service was already converted, but this PR changes the service too

The description states the Prisma.sql conversion was 'previously converted in the service implementation' and that this PR only updates tests. The diff, however, rewrites insightsBooking.ts (new SQL-building logic, removed findMany, changed types and constructor option type). Reviewers relying on the description would under-scope the review of the high-risk authorization SQL.
